Most gallstones in cholelithiasis are composed of what?
ch: Uric acid stones related to hyperuricemia and gout
Protein and bile salt plugs formed purely from bile stasis
Cholesterol stones, which make up roughly 75% of gallstones
Pigment stones, seen with hemolysis, cirrhosis, or infection
Calcium oxalate crystals, as in renal stone disease

questions.q: Acute calculous cholecystitis results most directly from which event?
ch: A stone lodged in the common bile duct with rising bilirubin
Bile stasis and ischemia in a fasting, critically ill patient
Ascending bacterial infection of the intrahepatic bile ducts
A stone impacted in the cystic duct, causing wall edema and distension
A stone eroding through the wall into the adjacent small bowel

questions.q: The classic “5 F's” mnemonic for cholelithiasis risk stands for which set of factors?
ch: Family history, Fluid overload, Fever, Fatigue, Fainting
Fat intolerance, Fetor, Fissure, Fibroma, Frequency

questions.q: Which examination finding is described as Murphy’s sign?
ch: Pain on passive extension of the right hip with the knee flexed
Flank ecchymosis appearing two to three days after symptom onset
A palpable, nontender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient
Rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant at McBurney’s point
Inspiratory arrest on deep RUQ palpation, sensitive for acute cholecystitis

questions.q: RUQ ultrasound is first-line for suspected acute cholecystitis. Which combination of findings confirms it?
ch: A dilated common bile duct containing a filling defect on MRCP
Diffuse calcification of the gallbladder wall without any stones
Stones, wall thickening over 3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign
Nonvisualization of the gallbladder after radiotracer administration
Pneumobilia with small-bowel obstruction on plain radiography

questions.q: When RUQ ultrasound is equivocal, which study is the most specific for acute cholecystitis?
ch: Repeat ultrasound in 24 hours after a fatty meal challenge
Abdominal plain films looking for a porcelain gallbladder
Serum lipase to exclude a coexisting gallstone pancreatitis
ERCP to visualize and clear the common bile duct
HIDA scan — nonvisualization of the gallbladder confirms cystic duct obstruction

questions.q: A patient has RUQ pain, fever, and jaundice together. Which diagnosis does this triad indicate?
ch: Acalculous cholecystitis in a critically ill patient
Cholangitis — Charcot's triad, which is not cholecystitis
Gallstone ileus with pneumobilia and bowel obstruction
Acute cholecystitis with a positive Murphy’s sign
Biliary colic triggered by a recent fatty meal

questions.q: A stable patient with mild acute cholecystitis has been resuscitated with IV fluids and started on antibiotics. What is the definitive management?
ch: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ideally within 72 hours
Ursodeoxycholic acid to dissolve the stones over several months
Percutaneous cholecystostomy as the definitive procedure
Delayed cholecystectomy after six weeks of oral antibiotics
ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction from the duct

questions.q: A critically ill post-op patient on TPN develops fever and RUQ pain, and ultrasound shows no stones. What is the likely diagnosis?
ch: Acalculous cholecystitis from bile stasis and ischemia
Biliary colic from a stone that has already passed
Mirizzi syndrome from a stone compressing the hepatic duct
Gallstone ileus from a stone eroding into the small bowel

questions.q: A patient admitted with acute cholecystitis develops markedly rising bilirubin and ALP with a dilated common bile duct. What does this suggest?
ch: Post-cholecystectomy syndrome from retained insufflated gas
Simple biliary colic that will resolve without intervention
Emphysematous cholecystitis with crepitus over the wall
Choledocholithiasis — obtain MRCP or ERCP for duct stones
Courvoisier's sign of malignant biliary obstruction

Which description most accurately characterizes ulcerative colitis?
ch: Transmural inflammation occurring anywhere from mouth to anus
Continuous mucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum and confined to the colon
Patchy inflammation involving the terminal ileum but sparing the colon
Granulomatous inflammation limited to the small intestine
Perianal fistulizing disease with skip lesions

questions.q: Which complication is most directly explained by the transmural nature of Crohn's disease?
Which presentation most strongly favors ulcerative colitis over Crohn's disease?
ch: Right lower-quadrant pain with a draining perianal fistula
Weight loss with terminal ileal inflammation
Bloody diarrhea with urgency and tenesmus
Recurrent bowel obstruction from a fibrotic stricture

questions.q: Which test is considered confirmatory for inflammatory bowel disease and helps distinguish ulcerative colitis from Crohn's disease?
A patient with known IBD presents with worsening diarrhea while receiving immunosuppressive therapy. Which step should occur before escalating immunosuppression?
ch: Schedule colectomy regardless of IBD subtype
Order ASCA testing to confirm an acute flare
Start an antidiarrheal agent before further evaluation

questions.q: Which statement about corticosteroid therapy in IBD is correct?
ch: Corticosteroids prevent postoperative Crohn's recurrence indefinitely
Corticosteroids should be stopped abruptly once symptoms improve
Corticosteroids are preferred for lifelong maintenance
Corticosteroids are used to induce remission during moderate or severe flares
Corticosteroids are curative in ulcerative colitis

questions.q: A patient with moderate-to-severe IBD is being evaluated for immunomodulator and biologic therapy. Which assessment set is most appropriate?
ch: Serum amylase, lipase, and troponin testing
Immediate biologic treatment without laboratory evaluation
Latent tuberculosis screening, hepatitis B testing, CBC/TPMT assessment, and exclusion of active infection

questions.q: A hospitalized patient with ulcerative colitis develops fever, tachycardia, marked abdominal distension, and colonic dilation greater than 6 cm. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
ch: Toxic megacolon requiring urgent medical and surgical evaluation
Mild ulcerative-colitis flare appropriate for outpatient mesalamine alone

questions.q: A patient with terminal ileal Crohn's disease is at increased risk for which combination?
ch: Vitamin C excess, uric-acid stones, and hypercalcemia
Iron overload, cholesterol deficiency, and nephrotic syndrome
Folate toxicity, pancreatic cancer, and cystinuria
Vitamin A excess, pigment stones, and respiratory alkalosis
Vitamin B12 deficiency, gallstones, and calcium-oxalate kidney stones

questions.q: A patient has had extensive ulcerative colitis for nine years and also has primary sclerosing cholangitis. Which management principle is most appropriate?
ch: Use ASCA levels as the primary colorectal cancer screening test
Delay colorectal cancer surveillance until symptoms worsen
Begin or continue surveillance colonoscopy because risk increases with disease duration, with earlier surveillance warranted in PSC
Use corticosteroids indefinitely to prevent colorectal cancer
Reassure the patient that colectomy cannot cure ulcerative colitis

questions.q: What best describes diverticulosis?
ch: Mucosal and submucosal outpouchings through the muscular wall without inflammation

questions.q: The most common location of diverticulitis is the:
Which mechanism most commonly initiates acute diverticulitis?
ch: Obstruction of a diverticulum with subsequent microperforation

questions.q: Which combination is the classic presentation of uncomplicated diverticulitis?
Preferred imaging study?
Characteristic CT finding?
Management of a 4-cm pericolic abscess?
Which statement about antibiotics is correct?
ch: Mild uncomplicated disease in selected immunocompetent patients may be managed without routine antibiotics

questions.q: Which Hinchey stage represents generalized fecal peritonitis?
Best long-term recurrence prevention?
ch: High-fiber diet, exercise, smoking cessation, and weight management

questions.q: Which is the first priority in suspected bowel obstruction?
ch: Resuscitation with IV fluids, bowel rest, and decompression

questions.q: The most common cause of adult small bowel obstruction is:
Preferred imaging study?
Which finding raises concern for strangulation?
Typical proximal SBO symptom?
Perforation risk rises once cecal diameter exceeds approximately:
When is nonoperative management appropriate?
Which medication class should generally be avoided in fixed mechanical obstruction?
Which complication most directly results from impaired bowel perfusion?
The best summary principle is:
ch: Resuscitate, decompress, assess, decide, act early

questions.q: Which description best characterizes Clostridioides difficile and how it produces colitis?
ch: A Gram-negative rod that invades the small bowel mucosa and elaborates a heat-labile enterotoxin
A Gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobe that overgrows the colon after antibiotics disrupt the gut microbiota
A protozoan parasite acquired from contaminated water that adheres to the duodenal brush border
A Gram-positive coccus that forms a preformed toxin in food and produces vomiting within a few hours
An enveloped virus that destroys villous enterocytes and produces osmotic diarrhea in institutional outbreaks

questions.q: Toxin A and toxin B produce C. difficile colitis primarily by which mechanism?
ch: Activating adenylate cyclase to produce a purely secretory, non-inflammatory watery diarrhea
Fermenting unabsorbed carbohydrate in the colonic lumen to produce an osmotic diarrhea
Blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction of colonic smooth muscle
Cleaving mucosal IgA so that luminal flora invade the submucosa and bloodstream directly
Disrupting the colonocyte cytoskeleton, causing inflammation, fluid secretion, and pseudomembranes

questions.q: Which infection-control approach is required for a hospitalized patient with C. difficile colitis?
ch: Standard precautions only, because C. difficile spores are not transmitted from patient to patient
Alcohol-based hand gel after every contact, which is sufficient to kill C. difficile spores
Airborne precautions with a fitted N95 respirator for everyone who enters the patient's room
Contact precautions with soap-and-water hand hygiene and bleach (sporicidal) equipment cleaning
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask and routine quaternary-ammonium surface disinfection

questions.q: Per the IDSA/ACG guidance cited in the module, which agent is preferred first-line for an initial episode of C. difficile infection?
ch: Oral metronidazole 500 mg three times daily
Bezlotoxumab given as a single-agent infusion
Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily

questions.q: A resident orders intravenous vancomycin for a patient with confirmed C. difficile colitis. Why is this order wrong?
ch: Intravenous vancomycin is active only against the hypervirulent NAP1/BI/027 strain
Intravenous vancomycin is inactivated by colonic anaerobes before it can bind toxin
Intravenous vancomycin does not reach the colonic lumen, so it has no activity in C. difficile infection
Intravenous vancomycin works only when bezlotoxumab is infused at the same time
Intravenous vancomycin causes an ileus that raises the risk of toxic megacolon

questions.q: A patient with C. difficile infection has a WBC of 22,000 and a creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL, with a normal blood pressure, no ileus, and no colonic dilation. How is this episode classified?
Why does the module direct clinicians to avoid loperamide and other antimotility agents in C. difficile colitis?
ch: They bind oral vancomycin in the gut and lower its luminal concentration
They accelerate transit and wash fidaxomicin out of the colon before it can act
They impair clearance of toxin, risking ileus and toxic megacolon
They cause a disulfiram-like reaction when combined with metronidazole
They stimulate the hypervirulent NAP1/BI/027 strain to shed more spores

questions.q: Which statement about C. difficile stool testing reflects the diagnostic stewardship the module teaches?
ch: Formed stool should be sent for testing whenever a hospitalized patient has recently received antibiotics
A test-of-cure should be sent at the end of therapy to document microbiologic eradication before discharge
A toxin EIA on its own is the confirmatory test of choice in every hospitalized patient who has diarrhea
Test only symptomatic patients and do not perform a test-of-cure, because PCR stays positive after recovery
Colonoscopy looking for pseudomembranes is the routine first-line test used to confirm the diagnosis

questions.q: Which statement best describes the role of bezlotoxumab in C. difficile infection?
ch: An oral macrocyclic antibiotic that replaces vancomycin in the treatment of fulminant colitis
A live biotherapeutic product that restores microbiota diversity after multiply recurrent disease
A toxin-binding resin taken with meals to neutralize toxin A within the colonic lumen
A first-line single agent for the treatment of an initial episode of non-severe infection
A monoclonal antibody against toxin B used as an adjunct to prevent recurrence in high-risk patients

questions.q: On hospital day 4 of oral vancomycin for C. difficile infection, a patient's stool output falls sharply while the abdomen becomes distended with absent bowel sounds and the blood pressure drops to 84/50. What does this picture most likely represent?
ch: Recurrent infection that will need a tapered vancomycin course started at discharge
Ileus with fulminant colitis and possible toxic megacolon — a surgical emergency
An unrelated small-bowel obstruction manageable with nasogastric suction alone
Expected clinical improvement, since falling stool frequency is the best marker of response
Vancomycin-induced constipation that should be relieved with a stimulant laxative
